keyIdeas.statement: Everything is made of tiny particles that are always moving.
keyIdeas.explanation: The particles are far too small to see, but their arrangement and movement decide whether a substance is a solid, a liquid or a gas.
keyIdeas.example: A drop of ink spreads through still water because water particles are moving and jostle the ink particles apart.
keyIdeas.analogy: Pupils standing still in rows are a solid; walking around a room a liquid; running around the playground a gas.

keyIdeas.statement: Heating gives particles energy; cooling takes it away, and that is what changes the state.
keyIdeas.explanation: Energy makes particles move more and spread out; losing energy lets them settle closer together. Melting, boiling, condensing and freezing are the same particles with more or less energy.
keyIdeas.example: Steam from a kettle turns back to water drops on a cold window because the gas particles lose energy and gather together.

misconceptions.belief: Particles in a solid do not move at all.
misconceptions.correction: They vibrate on the spot; only a gas has particles that move freely.

misconceptions.belief: When water boils, the bubbles are made of air.
misconceptions.correction: The bubbles are water as a gas; the liquid's own particles have gained enough energy to escape.

vocabulary.definition: A very small piece of a substance, too small to see.
A state in which particles are packed closely and only vibrate.
A state in which particles touch but can move past each other.
A state in which particles are far apart and move freely.
The change of state from solid to liquid on heating.
The change of state from gas to liquid on cooling.

workedExamples.problem: Why does an ice cube left on a plate turn into a puddle?
steps: Room air is warmer than the ice, so energy passes into the ice.
The particles gain energy and vibrate more strongly.
They break free of their fixed positions and can slide past each other.
workedExamples.answer: The ice melts: its particles gain energy and it changes from a solid to a liquid.

questions.stem: In which state of matter are the particles furthest apart?
questions.reasoning: Gas particles have large gaps between them and move freely.

distractors.text: They are the same in every state

questions.stem: What is the change of state from liquid to gas called?
questions.reasoning: Particles gain enough energy to escape the liquid as a gas.

questions.stem: True or false: particles in a solid do not move at all.
Put these in order of increasing particle energy: gas, solid, liquid.
questions.reasoning: Energy rises from solid through liquid to gas.

questions.stem: What happens to the particles in a liquid when it is heated to boiling?
questions.answer: They gain energy and move far apart to become a gas.
questions.reasoning: Boiling is the liquid-to-gas change; particles escape the liquid.

questions.stem: Describe how particles are arranged in a solid.
questions.answer: Packed closely in fixed positions, vibrating.
questions.reasoning: The fixed arrangement is why a solid keeps its shape.

questions.stem: Why can you pour a liquid but not a solid?
questions.answer: Liquid particles can slide past each other; solid particles cannot.
questions.reasoning: Movement of particles decides whether the substance flows.

questions.stem: What are the bubbles in boiling water made of?
questions.reasoning: The liquid's own particles have gained enough energy to escape.

questions.stem: Name the change of state from gas to liquid.
questions.reasoning: Cooling takes energy from gas particles so they gather together.

questions.stem: A sealed balloon is warmed in the sun. What happens to the gas particles inside and to the balloon?
questions.answer: The particles move faster and spread out, so the balloon expands.
questions.reasoning: More energy means faster particles pushing on the balloon skin.

questions.stem: Why does a puddle disappear on a warm day even though the water never boils?
questions.answer: Particles at the surface gain enough energy to escape as a gas, a little at a time.
questions.reasoning: Evaporation happens below the boiling point at the surface.

questions.stem: Explain why a metal spoon stays solid in hot tea but butter melts.
questions.answer: Metal particles need far more energy to break from their positions than butter particles do.
questions.reasoning: Different substances change state at different temperatures.

questions.stem: Which change of state happens when a gas cools down?
questions.reasoning: Losing energy lets gas particles gather into a liquid.
